solutions.check: 26 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Toady: "Credit to eccentric Nige!"

indicators.note: an eccentric person behaves oddly, so these letters are set out in an odd new order

blocks.note: CR is the standard abbreviation for credit on a statement
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A sycophant gushing praise at Nigel Farage, called by his nickname Nige.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toady' reads as a noun naming the speaker, but it is the verb: to fawn or grovel.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe, in an older sense, is to behave obsequiously and fawn on someone powerful, which is what toadying means.

clue.text: Grayling, hard to be got rid of, is a disaster

indicators.note: whatever is got rid of is thrown out, so a letter disappears from the name

blocks.note: Chris Grayling, the Conservative cabinet minister, supplies his first name
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard; this letter is removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A jibe that the minister Chris Grayling, notorious for blunders, is himself a calamity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname stands for the forename: Chris Grayling was a Tory transport secretary much mocked in Private Eye. Drop H from CHRIS and add IS.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is a moment of acute trouble or calamity, a close synonym for a disaster.

clue.text: Element of gash in boner – you wouldn't want to be kicked there

definitions.text: you wouldn't want to be kicked there

indicators.note: an element is a component part, so the answer is one portion of the following run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, dropping the outer G, A and R

explanation.surface: A crude Private Eye image of an injury to the groin, followed by a wince.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface steers toward the groin, but the leg bone at the front of the shin is the painful spot meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The shinbone, or tibia, sits right under the skin at the front of the leg, so a kick there hurts sharply.

clue.text: (& 19dn.) Suffered defeat: perplexed, crushed

blocks.note: someone perplexed is at a loss
coffee beans that are crushed in a mill are said to have been reduced this way

explanation.surface: A beaten side, baffled and flattened after a loss.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 4 and 19 down; each half comes from one adjective after the colon.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose ground is to give way to an opponent or fall back in a contest, a form of being beaten.

clue.text: Popular with surfers, Bury – clear?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase rather than a noun: the thing that is popular with surfers

blocks.note: to inter is to bury a body
to clear a sum after deductions is to net it

explanation.surface: A question whether the Lancashire town of Bury, liked by wave riders, has good weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury looks like the town but is the verb, and the surfers are web surfers, not those at the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: People who browse the web are said to surf it, so the online network is the place web surfers favour.

clue.text: (&21dn.) Give excuse not to go to work: "Prick rot's bad – without energy"

definitions.text: Give excuse not to go to work

indicators.note: something gone bad is spoilt and out of shape, so these letters lose their order
without in its old sense means outside, so these letters sit around another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A worker's lame excuse for staying home: a nasty, listless infection after a prick.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 6 across and 21 down. 'Without' means outside here, so E goes inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To report sick is to tell an employer you are ill and cannot come in, an excuse for missing work.

clue.text: MP Roger's off with morning hidden agenda

indicators.note: food that is off has gone wrong, so these letters are disordered
something hidden is tucked away inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
AM, ante meridiem, marks the morning hours

explanation.surface: A politician called Roger slips away early in the day with a secret plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden agenda' looks like one phrase, but 'hidden' belongs to the wordplay and 'agenda' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme is a planned list of items or events, which is what an agenda sets out.

clue.text: Cast out: what Charles is after, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: the phrase asks the solver to go by how a word is heard rather than written

blocks.note: Prince Charles, heir for decades, was waiting for the royal seat

explanation.surface: A wry dig at Prince Charles's long wait to succeed his mother.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue predates Charles's accession: as Prince of Wales he was waiting to become king.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrown is the past participle of throw, and something cast out has been flung or tossed away.

clue.text: President's no.1 alternative rejected – spot and pressure woman for sex?

indicators.note: number one in a line is the first, so only the opening letter counts
something rejected is sent back, so the word is turned round

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
or is the word that offers an alternative
a spot is a place or position

explanation.surface: A presidential sex scandal: the man in charge spots a woman and leans on her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like a verb meaning notice, but it is the noun for a place. The question mark flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To proposition someone is to make them an unwelcome sexual offer, which the clue paints as pressuring a woman.

clue.text: See 22ac.
Tip of todger trapped in Gents somehow? In that case, support

indicators.note: a tip is an extremity, here the far end, so only the final letter is kept
somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters come out in an unknown order
whatever is trapped is shut inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written, then rearranged
then can mean in that case, as in 'then we'll go'

explanation.surface: A smutty Private Eye scene of a zip accident in a men's lavatory, with an athletic support suggested as the remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' suggests the front end, but it is the last letter of todger, British slang for penis. Gents is a British word for a men's toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To strengthen something is to reinforce or bolster it, which is to give it support.

clue.text: Sheeran's backing prominent "nothing's out" Brexiteer? Rubbish

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the letters run the other way
something out has been removed, so that letter leaves the name

blocks.note: Ed Sheeran is the singer
only describes the Brexiteer
Boris Johnson led the Leave campaign
the round figure nothing looks like the letter O; this is removed

explanation.surface: Ed Sheeran endorses a leading Brexit campaigner's 'no deal' line, and the verdict is: rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as support, but it turns the singer's name round. 'Nothing's out' sounds like a Brexit slogan; it removes O.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is scattered waste or remains, a straightforward synonym for rubbish.

clue.text: Weighty Trump's ultimate gold-backed money supply contains zilch

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the closing letter is used
backed means pushed into reverse, so the letters run the other way
to contain is to hold inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the final letter of the name
OR is gold in heraldry
a fund is a supply of money
zilch is nothing, a zero, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: A jibe at Trump's economics: a gold-standard money plan that adds up to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weighty Trump' reads as a remark about his size, but 'Weighty' is the definition standing alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Profound thoughts carry great depth and seriousness, which is the figurative sense of weighty.

clue.text: Acted like a non-compliant judge, or a too eager Brenda?

definitions.note: a noun phrase describing the person who over-ruled, not a verb

blocks.note: first meaning: a judge who will not go along with an objection rejects it
second meaning, split in two: a queen too keen on reigning ruled to excess

explanation.surface: A comparison between a stubborn judge and an overzealous Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. Read the answer as over-ruled: ruled too much.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge who overrules sets aside an objection or earlier decision, refusing to comply with it; a monarch rules, and an over-eager one would rule excessively.

clue.text: Undistinguished Miliband's back, undertaking to present a big blow to May

indicators.note: going back means travelling in reverse, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: common means ordinary, nothing special
Ed Miliband, former Labour leader, with the possessive S
a feat is a notable undertaking or achievement

explanation.surface: Ed Miliband returns to the front line with a plan to wound Theresa May.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as a comeback, but it reverses the name with its possessive S. May is Theresa May, the prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa May lost several key votes on her Brexit deal in the House of Commons in 2019, each a heavy parliamentary loss.

clue.text: Singer – rich yob going bananas about nothing

indicators.note: going bananas means going crazy, so these letters are scrambled
about means around, so these letters surround another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
nothing is zero, written like the letter O

explanation.surface: A wealthy lout with a singing career throws a tantrum over nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The rich yob suggests a pop star, but the singer turns out to be an innocent church chorister. Yob is British slang for a thug.
explanation.definitionFit: A choirboy is a boy who sings in a church choir, so he is a kind of singer.

clue.text: One enters working member of labouring class as "free but with strings attached"

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a means one, as in a single thing
a machine that is working is on
prole, short for proletarian, is a working-class person

explanation.surface: A labourer is described as at liberty only under conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: The working and labouring in the surface suggest a job, but 'working' supplies a short word and 'One' is the inserted letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner released on parole is out of jail but must obey conditions, so the freedom has strings attached.

clue.text: Many would find it attractive to phone about securing May's end

indicators.note: about can mean astir or out of place, so these letters are moved around
to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so one piece grips another
an end is the last part, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: A suggestion that lots of people would like to ring Theresa May and hasten her departure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' but scrambles the letters, and 'May' is the prime minister, not the month.
explanation.definitionFit: A honeypot is a place or thing that draws crowds, like bees to honey, so it is widely attractive.

clue.text: Get on after skirt pulled back – that's not what it seems

indicators.note: pulled back means drawn in reverse, so the letters run the other way
after places the first-named piece behind the second, so the clue's order is swapped in the answer

blocks.note: to skirt is to edge, and a rim is an edge
to get on is to grow older, or age

explanation.surface: A seedy scene of someone making a move once a skirt is lifted, with a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt' suggests clothing but means a border, and 'Get on' means grow old rather than proceed.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, such as false water in a desert: something that looks real but is not.

clue.text: Woe is me, mistakenly on right – butt of party

indicators.note: a thing done mistakenly is done wrong, so these letters come out in the wrong order
a butt is the thick back end, so only the last letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
R is the abbreviation for right
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lament from someone who sided with the right and became the party's laughing stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woe is me' looks like a single phrase, but 'Woe' alone is the definition and 'is me' is the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Woe and misery both mean deep unhappiness or distress, so the two are plain synonyms.

clue.text: See 4dn.
Rank and file party supporters betray radicals

blocks.note: to grass is British slang for informing on someone
radical comes from the Latin for root, and in maths a radical is a root

explanation.surface: Ordinary party members turn on the extremists in their ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: To grass is British slang for informing to the police. 'Radicals' suggests extremists, but it means roots, as in square roots.
explanation.definitionFit: The grass roots are the ordinary members of a political party, as opposed to its leadership.

clue.text: See 6ac.
(& 10ac.) Probe peer having it on rocks

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, so these letters are jolted out of order

blocks.note: to peer is to gaze closely at something
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An inquiry into a member of the House of Lords who is drinking whisky on the rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 22 and 10 across. 'Peer' suggests a lord, but it is the verb; 'on the rocks' suggests a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To look into a matter is to investigate it, the same sense as to probe an affair.

clue.text: Hidden sources of Conservative unrest welcomed by stupid clot

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so each word yields its opening letter
a guest who is welcomed is taken in, so one piece goes inside another
something stupid is muddled, so these letters lose their sense and order

blocks.note: the word itself, then rearranged
the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Secret origins of Tory discontent are blamed on a foolish blunderer who embraced them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden' sits at the front like a description of the sources, but it is the definition. Clot is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Occult originally meant concealed or secret, from Latin for covered over, a sense still used in medicine and astronomy.

clue.text: Date with limp, nerdy versifier

indicators.note: something limp has lost its firm shape, so these letters fall into a new arrangement

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for date
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A lacklustre romantic evening with a geeky poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' suggests a romantic outing, but it is just its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dryden was the seventeenth-century English poet laureate, so he is an example of a writer of verse.
